messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj is a 41-year-old South Asian male who works as an architect and is married. His journey into seeking help began after years of living with debilitating symptoms following physical abuse by his romantic partner. Raj describes the traumatic event vividly: he remembers the sharp pain, the scent of alcohol on his abuser’s breath, and the incomprehensible chatter that followed each assault. In the aftermath of these incidents, Raj found himself hypervigilant and easily startled. Even small triggers, such as feeling physically unwell or encountering the smell of alcohol, would plunge him back into a state of intense anxiety. These triggers were potent because they reminded him of the violent episodes and his body's immediate reaction to danger. He had come to believe that his body responded before he could fully process what was happening, heightening his sense of vulnerability. Raj's memories of the event are particularly vivid; they flash back as snapshots in his mind, each moment a photograph that brings back the same terror he felt at the time. This photographic recall is not just a visual experience but an emotional one too. The smell of alcohol or incomprehensible chatter can instantly transport him to those moments of fear and helplessness. The intensity of these memories and triggers has reinforced his negative appraisals about himself and his role in life. Raj harbors deep self-doubt, believing that he cannot trust himself to do the right thing. He feels a profound sense of failure for not being able to protect himself or fulfill what he considers his most important roles as a husband and an architect. The betrayal by someone he trusted has left him feeling broken and unable to trust others. His negative appraisals contribute to his heightened threat perception, making it difficult for Raj to relax or feel safe in any situation. He feels constantly on guard, which exacerbates his startle response and sleep vigilance. This hypervigilant state makes him more prone to experiencing triggers, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of anxiety and fear. Raj’s work as an architect has been profoundly impacted by these symptoms. He often finds himself distracted or unable to concentrate during meetings, especially when someone's voice is slurred or the office scents remind him of alcohol. His performance at work has suffered, leading to increased stress and a sense that he is failing in his professional responsibilities. What finally brought Raj to seek help was a particularly distressing incident where he found himself overwhelmed by the smell of alcohol during an important client meeting. The vivid memories and intense fear made it impossible for him to continue working effectively, and he realized he needed support to manage these overwhelming symptoms. He is most afraid that he will not be able to overcome his fears and doubts, but he also hopes to regain a sense of control over his life and his work. Raj’s story is one of resilience amidst profound trauma. His journey towards healing involves acknowledging the ways in which his triggers, memories, negative appraisals, and heightened threat perceptions have intertwined to create a complex web of distress. Through therapy, he aims to break this cycle and regain a sense of trust and control over his life.
